verdicts.verdict_reason: The phenomenon is the Bahadur-Savage 1956 impossibility (any valid interval over a rich class is unbounded or has coverage 0), restated and refined in several 2020-2026 papers for iid sampling. The mechanism needed here is elementary: the sample misses an arbitrarily large unsampled unit with probability at least 1-n/G, and predictions cannot reveal it. I found no paper stating it for SRSWOR from a fixed finite population, and none with the explicit bound (1-alpha-n/G)/(1-n/G) or the 'predictions cannot help' remark. The binary/hypergeometric analogue (a Wald interval whose coverage can fall to about n/N) appears only as a search snippet attributed to Wang 2015.

verdicts.verdict_reason: Pieces exist but not the claim. (a) Hajek (1960) proved a necessary and sufficient max-squared-deviation (Lindeberg-type) condition for the asymptotic normality of the SRSWOR mean. Li-Ding (2017) and Bloznelis (1999, Student statistic under SRSWOR) use it asymptotically. (b) Potscher-Preinerstorfer (Econometric Theory 2025/2026) prove a sharp finite-sample boundary of the same type, in the Gaussian heteroskedastic regression model: a finite size-controlling critical value exists iff no leverage equals 1, and otherwise size is 1 for every critical value. (c) Carter-Schnepel-Steigerwald's effective number of clusters and Muller's robust t-test treat concentration across few clusters asymptotically. I found no paper giving an explicit boundary kappa*(n,G,alpha) from the hypergeometric miss probability for SRSWOR finite populations, nor the 'location-scale-equivariant valid iff kappa0 <= kappa*' dichotomy.

verdicts.verdict_reason: The method type (exact worst-case critical value over a class, attained at extreme configurations) is established for other classes. Szekely 2006 and Bakirov-Szekely give exact smallest t-type critical values over symmetric and Gaussian-scale-mixture classes with extremal sign-vertex configurations. Potscher-Preinerstorfer give the smallest valid critical value under heteroskedasticity. Romano-Wolf give finite-sample CIs over bounded support. For SRSWOR finite populations I found only asymptotic or concentration-based work (Bloznelis 1999, Li-Ding 2017, Freidling 2026, Waudby-Smith-Ramdas 2020). I found no exactly calibrated studentized difference-estimator interval over {kappa <= kappa0}. The comparators are known: Canay-Romano-Shaikh sign-change tests are exact only under symmetry (Dutz-Zhang 2025 show mean-zero admits no randomization test), and Hagemann/Ibragimov-Muller are asymptotic or Gaussian-scale-mixture. The 'worst case at few-point populations' step is not obviously inherited, because the kappa constraint is a nonconvex quadratic constraint, unlike the convex class used by Szekely. If true it is a substantive lemma, not a corollary.

what_remains_open: (1) F: an explicit sharp boundary kappa*(n,G,alpha) for SRSWOR from the hypergeometric miss probability, with the 'location-scale-equivariant interval valid below, none above' dichotomy. No paper was found. The necessity half (a sample that misses all k atypical clusters is constant, so an equivariant interval has zero length) looks like a routine corollary of the LEMMA argument; I did not verify it, and it is my own sketch, not a literature result. The sufficiency half is K. (2) K: exact finite-sample critical values c(n,G,kappa0,alpha) for the studentized difference-estimator interval over {kappa <= kappa0}, with worst case at few-point populations. This is a substantive theorem if the extremal-population step holds. The closest methods (Szekely, Potscher-Preinerstorfer) are in other models, so the exact extremal property is the real novelty and the part most worth checking by computer first. (3) LEMMA: the explicit finite-population bound with the predictions-do-not-help remark is open, but it is a routine corollary. (4) B: an exact minimax length at n <= 16 is open, probably a routine corollary of the known bounded-range CIs. D was not assessed.

verdicts.verdict_reason: The substance (any procedure valid over an unrestricted class must be unbounded with positive probability; a.s.-bounded intervals have zero coverage; predictions of unperturbed units cannot help) is the Bahadur-Savage (1956) / Gleser-Hwang (1987) / Dufour (1997) / Bertanha-Moreira impossibility, and auditing papers (Stark 2009 TIFS, SUITE) state the finite-population analogue informally: a single unaudited large value makes the total arbitrarily large, so an a priori bound is required. I found no paper stating the finite-population version with the explicit hypergeometric constant. The argument is a one-line mixing/perturbation argument (shift one unit, which is unsampled with probability 1-n/G). Note from my own quick derivation (not from literature): perturbing one unit j gives P_z(theta+M/G in C, j unsampled) >= 1-alpha-n/G, i.e. the quoted (1-alpha-n/G)/(1-n/G) is the CONDITIONAL probability given j unsampled; the unconditional bound is 1-alpha-n/G unless the interval is argued conditionally. Worth rechecking before claiming.

verdicts.verdict_reason: The asymptotic version of the max-share quantity is classical: Erdos-Renyi (1959) and Hajek (1960) give a necessary and sufficient condition for asymptotic normality of the SRSWOR sample mean in terms of max (a_k - mu)^2 relative to total sum of squares (quoted in arXiv:0708.1880), with Berry-Esseen bounds for studentized finite-population means (Bloznelis 1999 and others) and Li-Ding (2017) CLTs. Muller's heavy-tail t-test paper makes the same 'one term dominates' point informally. None of these gives an exact finite-sample frontier kappa*(n,G,alpha) separating populations over which a location-scale-equivariant interval can/cannot be valid, linked to the hypergeometric miss probability C(G-k,n)/C(G,n). I found no such paper in my search, but the search is bounded (arXiv, web, partial Semantic Scholar) and the econometrics few-cluster literature was only lightly screened.

Scoop risk: moderate; the technique is standard so a competitor could do the finite-population version quickly. I did not read these papers' theorem sections beyond snippets.

Shekhar-Ramdas (arXiv:2603.14423) give a width lower bound only for finite alphabets in a moderate-accuracy asymptotic regime, and Shekhar-Ramdas 2310.01547 for iid; I found no exact small-n minimax for SRSWOR. verdicts.verdict_reason: Take-all (certainty) strata for skewed populations are classical in survey sampling: Dalenius (1952), Glasser (1962), Hidiroglou (1986), Lavallee-Hidiroglou (1988), Gunning-Horgan (2004), and Rivest (2002), who adapts the LH algorithm to a noisy/proxy stratification variable (log-linear change model or occasional large discrepancies), which is the 'cheap noisy first-phase measure' scenario; two-phase/Neyman-allocation theory covers the rest (Hedlin et al. on joint allocation and stratification). Those criteria minimize variance/sample size at a target CV, not a finite-sample validity (kappa*) criterion. If F is proved, picking the smallest take-all set that pushes remaining residual kappa below kappa* is a routine corollary of F plus stratified design, not a new theorem on its own. Read only abstracts/snippets of the survey-methodology papers.

what_remains_open: (1) F: an exact, explicit finite-sample frontier kappa*(n,G,alpha) for location-scale-equivariant intervals over {populations: max-share <= kappa0} under SRSWOR, tied to the hypergeometric miss probability; only the asymptotic Hajek/Erdos-Renyi max-share condition and Berry-Esseen-type bounds were found. This would be a substantive theorem if the sharpness (impossibility above, validity below) holds. (2) K: the exact critical value c(n,G,kappa0,alpha) for a studentized difference-estimator interval with worst case at few-atom populations, and its comparison to t, CR2 and CRS; the technique is standard (Hoeffding convex order + extremal few-point reduction), so the contribution would be a moderately substantive finite-population theorem with quick-follower risk. (3) B-minimax: exact small-n (n<=16) minimax interval length under SRSWOR with a known residual range; asymptotic/finite-alphabet lower bounds exist, an exact small-n statement does not look to be in print, but it is a routine-to-modest LP/duality computation. (4) LEMMA: the explicit quantitative n/G form is not found in print; it is a routine corollary of the classical impossibility (and see the conditional-vs-unconditional caveat). (5) D: only the validity-driven (kappa*) criterion for choosing the certainty stratum is not found; routine corollary of F.
other_relevant_findings: Three things in the neighbourhood that the project should cite or check. (a) The original PPI paper (Angelopoulos et al. 2023, App. B/E) already has the finite-population SRSWOR formulation with nonasymptotic bounded-residual intervals, so B cannot be framed as new; Mozer (arXiv:2603.19160) and Denis-Haddou (2026, J. verdicts.verdict_reason: The principle is classical and general: Bahadur-Savage (1956) for iid means; Gleser-Hwang (1987), Dufour (1997), Pfanzagl (1998) and Bertanha-Moreira (J. Econometrics 2020, Thm 3) prove that when the observed-data law is TV- (or Levy-Prokhorov-) close across parameter values, every valid confidence set must be unbounded with probability >= 1-alpha. In the finite-population design, the sample laws under z and z + M e_j differ in total variation by exactly P(j in S) = n/G, so the LEMMA is the quantitative (non-limiting) instance of that argument, and the 'predictions cannot help' remark is the same argument conditioning on the fixed f. Finite-population hypergeometric analogues exist for 0/1 values (a Wald-type interval's minimum coverage is at most n/N for rare-element populations), audit practice states that bounds on the values are needed unless a majority of batches is audited (Stark), and Basu's flat likelihood for unsampled units is the mechanism. I did not find a paper stating the SRSWOR mean-of-unbounded-values version with explicit n/G constant, but its proof is the one-line coupling above. NOTE a correction to the claim as worded: the argument gives P_z(theta + M/G in C) >= 1 - alpha - n/G unconditionally; the sharper (1-alpha-n/G)/(1-n/G) holds for the conditional probability given j not in S (sample misses unit j), not for the unconditional probability.

verdicts.verdict_reason: The ingredients are published but the specific finite-sample, design-based frontier is not. (i) Max-share of squared deviations is the Hajek/Lindeberg-Erdos-Renyi condition for SRSWOR CLTs (Hajek 1960; Li-Ding 2017; Bloznelis 1999 gives Berry-Esseen for the finite-population Student statistic under minimal such conditions; Hu et al. give relative-error bounds in max|a_k - mu|). (ii) Chiang-Sasaki-Wang (2023) give an asymptotic necessary-and-sufficient condition (largest cluster's score negligible) for valid cluster-robust t inference and show it fails often; Kojevnikov-Song (2023) give impossibility for variance estimation with one large cluster. (iii) For iid data a finite-sample boundary of the claimed type exists for the t interval (Hendriks et al. 2006: no bounded t-based interval with nominal coverage when n < 1 - log(alpha)/log 2, Bernoulli worst case), and Edelman (2025) finds k-sparse equal-weight extremals for the self-normalized sum under sign symmetry. (iv) Hypergeometric miss-all-k probabilities as a coverage ceiling appear for 0/1 populations (Wang). I found no paper that states a sharp explicit kappa*(n,G,alpha) for SRSWOR with location-scale-equivariant intervals, nor the 'valid below, impossible above' dichotomy; the 'impossible above' half looks like a short argument (two-point populations with k atypical units have constant samples with probability C(G-k,n)/C(G,n), so an equivariant interval has degenerate length there), while the 'valid below' half is claim K.

verdicts.verdict_reason: Finite-sample valid CIs for the mean of a bounded finite population under SRSWOR are standard: Hoeffding-Serfling (Serfling 1974), Hoeffding-Serfling and empirical Bernstein-Serfling (Bardenet-Maillard 2015), betting/e-process CIs and CSs without replacement (Waudby-Smith-Ramdas 2020; Martinez-Taboada-Ramdas 2026 with a WoR Gaussian-bridge version), and Shekhar-Ramdas (2026) with a lower bound on the width of any valid WoR CI. Because the PPI difference estimator with fixed lambda is the sample mean of residuals e_g = z_g - lambda f_g plus a known constant, applying any of these to residuals with a known range bound gives the few-cluster PPI interval as a corollary; Mozer (2026) establishes PPI = difference estimator, and Aronow-Lopatto / Hodges-Lehmann cover minimax point estimation under bounds. The part not found: an exact minimax-length (not MSE) statement for CIs at n <= 16 and alpha = 0.05; Shekhar-Ramdas' lower bound is for the large-deviation 'moderate accuracy' regime (log(1/alpha) >> (k+1) log N) so does not cover it. That remainder looks like a routine finite computation (LP over finite alphabets) rather than a deep theorem.

verdicts.verdict_reason: Take-all (certainty) strata for skewed populations with a cheap first-phase size/proxy measure are a long-standing survey-design topic: Dalenius 1952 and Glasser 1962 cut-offs, Hidiroglou 1986 (construction of a self-representing stratum), Lavallee-Hidiroglou 1988, Rivest 2002 (model in which the survey variable departs from the stratification variable for some units), Hedlin and the R 'stratification' package, plus two-phase sampling and robust estimators for influential units (Beaumont-Haziza-Ruiz-Gazen 2013; Beaumont-Rivest 2009). what_remains_open: (1) F/K: a finite-sample, design-based (SRSWOR) statement that a location-scale-equivariant interval is valid over all populations with max-share kappa <= kappa0 exactly when kappa0 is below a hypergeometric-miss threshold kappa*(n,G,alpha), with an explicit exactly-computable critical value attained at few-distinct-value populations; I found only asymptotic analogues (Hajek/Lindeberg, Chiang-Sasaki-Wang), iid analogues (Hendriks et al., Basu-DasGupta, Edelman sign-symmetric), and hypergeometric ceilings for 0/1 values (Wang). The 'impossible above kappa*' half appears routine (two-point populations / constant samples); the 'valid below with exact critical value' half is a substantive theorem plus computation, using standard extreme-point methods, and its novelty rests on my not having read Basu-DasGupta, Pinelis, Bakirov-Szekely in full. (2) B: an exact minimax confidence-interval length at n <= 16, alpha = 0.05 under SRSWOR with bounded residuals (routine computation). (3) D: a take-all rule defined by a validity boundary kappa* rather than a variance target (corollary-level once F/K exist). (4) LEMMA: only the explicit SRSWOR constant and its use with fixed predictions are unpublished in what I found; it is a routine corollary of the TV argument (and the stated constant needs the conditional-on-miss reading noted).
other_relevant_findings:
- Statement check: the argument yields P_z(theta+M/G in C) >= 1-alpha-n/G unconditionally; the (1-alpha-n/G)/(1-n/G) form is the conditional probability given the sample misses unit j. Unboundedness with positive probability then follows from limsup of the events {theta+M/G in C}.
- No finite-population or design-based PPI paper found containing an impossibility, minimax-CI or max-share result. PPI limits found are MSE-based (Mani et al. 2025: PPI++ beats gold-standard only above a correlation threshold of order 1/sqrt(n)), efficiency-based (Lee-Kim 2026, asymptotic) or empirical few-label observations (Eyre-Madras 2025). Mozer (2026) already identifies PPI with the survey difference estimator, so the survey-sampling framing cannot be claimed as new.

- Heavy-tailed side: median-of-means/Catoni give CIs only with a known variance or moment bound (stated in Gasparin-Ramdas 2024 excerpt; Bhatt et al. title seen only in a reference list); this is the heavy-tail analogue of the LEMMA and would be the natural comparator for any 'known bound' variant.

I found no paper giving a finite-sample, finite-population (SRSWOR), kappa-constrained studentized-difference interval with exactly computed c(n,G,kappa0,alpha). If correct this would be a substantive theorem (extremal-point reduction under SRSWOR with a max-share constraint is not routine), but the analogy to Pinelis/PP is strong, so novelty is mostly in the finite-population/design-based setting and PPI application. what_remains_open: Within my theme, what no paper covers: (1) a finite-sample, SRSWOR finite-population interval whose validity region is indexed by the max-share kappa(e) of residuals and whose critical value c(n,G,kappa0,alpha) is exact (worst case over all populations with kappa<=kappa0, attained at few-valued populations) - this is the only substantive theorem-level remainder (K/F-sharpness), and I have not verified it is true; it would be a finite-population, design-based analogue of Potscher-Preinerstorfer Thm 2.2 / Pinelis two-point extremal results. (2) The explicit hypergeometric form of the finite-population Bahadur-Savage bound (1-alpha-n/G)/(1-n/G) and the 'predictions cannot help because f_j is unchanged' remark - elementary corollary, no explicit statement found, likely regarded as folklore. (3) Any minimax length claim for bounded-residual PPI at n<=16 - not found, minor. (4) A kappa-based criterion for the certainty stratum - routine corollary once F/K are proved. Broska-Howes explicitly leave few-cluster small-sample corrections to future work, so cluster-robust PPI with few clusters is open, but their forward citations could not be enumerated.
other_relevant_findings: (a) Potscher-Preinerstorfer arXiv:2412.17470 Thm 2.2 is the closest structural precedent (iff leverage condition + smallest size-controlling critical value, finite sample) and must be cited. (b) Kojevnikov-Song and Chiang-Sasaki-Wang: single/largest-cluster impossibility and iff-normality conditions in the econometrics few/large-cluster literature. (c) Pinelis 2006 two-point mixture representation and Efron/Eaton/Bakirov-Szekely: worst-case t over a class is at few-point laws. (d) CRS sign-change tests cannot reject at 5% with fewer than 6 clusters (minimum p-value grid), a fact that disposes of that comparator at n=4-5. (e) Denis-Haddou 2026 'Prediction-Powered Estimation' (design-based PPI for survey designs, unbiased variance) and arXiv:2608.10356 (design-based PPI for spatial finite populations) show the finite-population PPI framing is already in print; arXiv:2606.08730 documents PPI small-label undercoverage. (f) Gafarov-Ura 2603.24786 (skewness-aware few-cluster critical values) corroborates that few-cluster skew correction exists in econometrics. (g) Valliant-Rust 2010 / Stata svy docs: survey practice already notes d.f.=PSUs-strata is liberal under skewness and few PSUs.

verdicts.verdict_reason: The mechanism (two sample laws at total-variation distance n/G from each other, so any procedure valid over all populations is unbounded with positive probability) is the Bahadur-Savage 1956 argument and its TV-distance generalisations (Dufour 1997; Bertanha-Moreira). Auditing/finite-population papers state that a known bound is required for SRSWOR (Bentkus-van Zuijlen 2003; Stark/Kaplan-Wald; Romano-Wolf; Shekhar-Ramdas 2026 'any valid WoR CI' lower bound; Zhu-Duchi 2026). I did NOT find a paper that states the explicit finite-population inequality (1-alpha-n/G)/(1-n/G) or the 'predictions cannot help because f_j is unchanged' remark; both are routine corollaries of the TV argument with TV = P(j in S) = n/G.

verdicts.verdict_reason: Components exist separately: (i) max-share kappa is the Hajek/Erdos-Renyi Lindeberg-type quantity (Hajek 1960; Li-Ding 2017 m_N/v_N), with finite-n Berry-Esseen bounds for the studentized SRSWOR mean (Hoglund 1978; Rao-Zhao 1994; Bloznelis 1999) and the 'effective number of clusters' of Carter-Schnepel-Steigerwald in econometrics; (ii) the hypergeometric probability C(G-k,n)/C(G,n) of missing all k units is classical (rule-of-three / exact hypergeometric CIs). None of these gives a sharp boundary kappa*(n,G,alpha) separating existence from non-existence of finite-sample-valid location-scale-equivariant intervals; those results are asymptotic or approximate and say nothing about impossibility above a threshold. In my survey-sampling search I found no paper proving such a frontier. Cochran's rule n>25*G1^2 (Sugden-Smith-Jones) is the nearest 'restriction vs n' statement but is Edgeworth-asymptotic and moment-based, not an exact validity boundary.

verdicts.verdict_reason: No survey-sampling paper gives an exactly calibrated studentized difference-estimator interval for SRSWOR populations restricted by kappa<=kappa0. Nearest technical precedents: Rosenblum-van der Laan 2009 (inflate a preliminary CI by the smallest factor guaranteeing coverage over ALL laws in a model class, worst case located numerically, iid/parametric class, no max-share restriction); Pinelis 1994/2006 and Eaton-Efron (exact conservative self-normalised-sum bounds, extremal laws are at-most-two-point mixtures, iid and symmetry/zero-mean rather than finite-population); Bakirov-Szekely/Ibragimov-Mueller (Gaussian clusters, t critical values valid under heterogeneity); Li et al. 2026 (exact worst-case tails under kurtosis with few-atom extremals, single variable). The worst-case-at-few-atoms mechanism is therefore known in spirit, but its application to the SRSWOR studentized PPI/difference statistic with an exact computable c(n,G,kappa0,alpha) was not found. Likely a real but technically moderate theorem (finite extreme-point/LP argument over hypergeometric samples).

verdicts.verdict_reason: Putting the largest units into a certainty (take-all) stratum identified from a cheap first-phase size/auxiliary measure is standard survey practice (Dalenius 1952; Glasser 1962; Hidiroglou 1986; Lavallee-Hidiroglou 1988; Rivest 2002; Benedetti-Bee-Espa 2010), including a model where the auxiliary variable matches the target for most units and large discrepancies occur for some units (Rivest 2002) and two-phase sampling since Neyman 1938; in PPI, active/uncertainty-proportional labelling gives probability near one to uncertain units. What I did not find is the specific criterion: the smallest take-all stratum such that the remaining residual max-share falls below a finite-sample validity boundary kappa*. Existing take-all rules minimise cost for a target CV, not CI validity. If F exists, D is a routine corollary (greedy removal of largest |e_g - ebar|).

what_remains_open: (1) F: the sharp boundary kappa*(n,G,alpha) for existence vs non-existence of finite-sample-valid location-scale-equivariant intervals over {kappa<=kappa0} was not found anywhere in survey sampling; pieces (Hajek-Lindeberg quantity, hypergeometric miss probability, Berry-Esseen bounds) are classical, so what is new would be the exact frontier theorem, a substantive result if proved. Econometrics/nonparametric theme checkers should confirm. (2) K: an exactly calibrated studentized SRSWOR difference-estimator interval with worst case at few-valued populations and exact c(n,G,kappa0,alpha); nearest are Rosenblum-van der Laan (iid, numerical inflation) and Pinelis (iid, symmetric/zero-mean). Likely a moderately technical but genuine theorem; comparison with CR2/CRS is empirical. (3) LEMMA: only the explicit (1-alpha-n/G)/(1-n/G) form and the 'predictions cannot help' remark are unlocated; a routine corollary of TV-based Bahadur-Savage. (4) B: only an exact n<=16 minimax-length statement; routine/computational. (5) D: only the kappa*-based certainty-stratum criterion; routine corollary once F holds.
other_relevant_findings: Survey-sampling papers with finite-sample guarantees for skewed populations under a stated restriction: (a) Rosenblum & van der Laan 2009 (bounded range -> Bernstein CIs with guaranteed coverage; plus worst-case inflation over a parametric class) is the closest in spirit, and it explicitly motivates small numbers of clusters; (b) Bentkus-van Zuijlen 2003, Serfling 1974, Bardenet-Maillard 2015, Waudby-Smith-Ramdas 2020/2024 (known range); (c) Bloznelis 1999 / Hoglund 1978 / Rao-Zhao 1994 give finite-sample Berry-Esseen bounds for the studentized mean, which are error bounds rather than valid intervals. Everything else on skewed populations is asymptotic or empirical: Cochran's rule and Sugden-Smith-Jones 2000 (Edgeworth; its forward citations on Semantic Scholar include Qing-Valliant 2025 and Kott-Levine 2024, all asymptotic), Johnson 1978 / Hall 1992 transformations (iid), saddlepoint (Robinson 1982; Empirical saddlepoint studentized mean under SRS, 2001), pseudo-population bootstrap (Booth-Butler-Hall 1994), Polya posterior / weighted Polya posterior (Meeden 1999: improved but unguaranteed coverage), outlier-robust estimation (Chambers 1986; Kokic-Bell 1994; Beaumont-Haziza-Ruiz-Gazen 2013: MSE-oriented, no CI guarantee), and Korn-Graubard / Kott degrees-of-freedom rules for few PSUs (heuristic). Setting-level overlap: Mozer 2026 (arXiv:2603.19160) shows PPI mean = Cassel-Sarndal-Wretman difference estimator, so the survey-sampling reading of the problem is already public; PPI's own Appendix B already treats SRSWOR finite populations. New 2026 arXiv items worth tracking: Shekhar-Ramdas 2603.14423 (WoR width lower bound), Martinez-Taboada-Ramdas 2608.21694 (WoR betting), Li et al. 2607.05226 (exact worst-case tails under kurtosis), Zhu-Duchi 2609.05360 (finite-sample nonnegative-mean tests).
